presentingComplaint: Fever, rigors and a red, discharging swelling over the pacemaker site for 6 days.
history: Retired schoolteacher with a dual-chamber permanent pacemaker implanted 14 months ago for complete heart block. Currently 8 days into cycle 3 of R-CHOP chemotherapy for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, so he is immunocompromised. Over the past week he has had swinging fevers to 39C with drenching rigors, and has noticed the skin over the left infraclavicular generator pocket becoming red, tender and swollen, with a small amount of pus tracking from the incision line in the last 48 hours. He denies cough, dysuria, diarrhoea or abdominal pain. No recent dental work. His oncologist started him on oral co-amoxiclav 3 days ago with no improvement and worsening local signs. Comorbidities: type 2 diabetes, hypertension. He lives with his wife and had no prior device problems.
examination: Unwell, flushed and febrile. The left pre-pectoral pacemaker pocket is erythematous, warm, fluctuant and exquisitely tender, with skin thinning and serosanguinous-purulent discharge at the medial suture line; no frank device erosion through skin yet. No peripheral stigmata of endocarditis, no new murmur, chest clear, abdomen soft. No focal neurology. Mild oral mucositis from chemotherapy. Peripheral pulses intact.
imaging: Chest radiograph: pacemaker generator and two intact leads in situ, no pulmonary infiltrate. Transthoracic then transoesophageal echocardiography: no valvular vegetation, but a small mobile echodensity adherent to the ventricular lead in the right atrium consistent with lead vegetation; normal valve function. Pocket ultrasound: 3 cm rim-enhancing fluid collection around the generator.
microbiology: Two sets of peripheral blood cultures drawn before antibiotic change both flag positive at 14h and 16h for Gram-positive cocci in clusters; repeat cultures at 48h remain positive (persistent bacteraemia). Final identification: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), vancomycin MIC 1.0 mg/L. Pocket pus Gram stain: Gram-positive cocci, same organism on culture. Urine culture negative.
differentialDiagnoses: CIED pocket infection with lead-associated bacteraemia (device infection)
finalDiagnosis: Cardiac implantable electronic device (CIED) infection: MRSA generator-pocket infection with lead vegetation and persistent bacteraemia in an immunocompromised host, requiring complete device and lead extraction.
citations: AHA Scientific Statement on Management of Cardiac Implantable Electronic Device Infections 2024
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 22e — Infections of Prosthetic Devices and Intravascular Catheters
stewardship: This is a device infection with pocket involvement, a lead vegetation and persistent MRSA bacteraemia in a chemotherapy-immunosuppressed patient. Because the host is immunocompromised and septic-appearing, start broad empiric IV cover with vancomycin (MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci) plus an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime) to cover Gram-negatives pending cultures. Once MRSA is confirmed and Gram-negatives excluded, de-escalate/narrow to targeted anti-staphylococcal therapy (vancomycin, or daptomycin if persistent bacteraemia) and stop cefepime. The cornerstone is source control: complete removal of the entire device system (generator and all leads) — antibiotics alone will not clear a device infection. Duration is counted from the day of extraction and negative blood cultures (typically 2-4 weeks for bacteraemia with lead vegetation). Obtain repeat cultures to document clearance before any reimplantation, and reassess need for a new device.
contraindications: Do not attempt to treat a CIED infection with antibiotics alone — complete device/lead extraction is mandatory.
Avoid nephrotoxic dosing errors of vancomycin given diabetes and borderline renal function; use AUC-guided monitoring.
Do not reimplant a device at the infected site or before documented blood-culture clearance.
edgeCases: If echocardiography had shown valve vegetation, this would reclassify as CIED-related infective endocarditis with longer therapy.
If the patient were profoundly neutropenic (ANC <500) at presentation, febrile-neutropenia protocols would run in parallel but the localised pocket source still defines device infection.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci from a single culture could be a contaminant, but concordant pocket and blood isolates confirm true infection here.
expectedMaiK: Fever with an inflamed, discharging pacemaker pocket plus persistent staphylococcal bacteraemia and a lead vegetation in an immunocompromised patient is a CIED infection mandating complete system extraction with targeted antibiotics, not antibiotics alone.
expectedNextQuestions: When was the device implanted or last manipulated, and were there any prior pocket problems or wound-healing issues?
Are there peripheral stigmata of endocarditis or a new murmur suggesting valve involvement?
What is the current chemotherapy cycle and neutrophil count / degree of immunosuppression?
Have blood cultures been taken from two separate sites before escalating antibiotics?
expectedInvestigations: Two sets of peripheral blood cultures before antibiotics, with repeat cultures to document clearance
Gram stain and culture of pocket aspirate/tissue (avoid superficial swab alone)
Transoesophageal echocardiography to assess for lead and valve vegetations
Full blood count with differential, CRP/procalcitonin, renal function
Device pocket ultrasound and consideration of PET-CT / lead-tip culture at extraction

Empiric regimen must include vancomycin for MRSA/CoNS cover in a septic immunocompromised host.
Management must flag complete device and lead extraction (source control) as mandatory, not antibiotics alone.
